entries.label: Bantu
entries.summary: A label for a large family of related languages. According to van der Waal (2011), it began as a linguistic label in a nineteenth-century grammar, built on a Zulu word for people. Later anthropology and apartheid-era policy used it as the name of distinct peoples, and many South Africans now find that use offensive. Yanovich (2025) reviews linguistic, archaeological and genetic work and cautions that current stories of Bantu history are not settled. Some sources, including the UNESCO record for Great Zimbabwe, still use the label for people.
entries.framing: Start with who applied the label, to whom, and for what purpose, before treating it as a neutral name. Ask how communities name themselves, and keep 'Bantu' as a language term unless a source for a specific use says otherwise.

sources.label: Kees van der Waal (2011), Bantu: From Abantu to Ubuntu
Igor Yanovich (2025), Reconstructing the Historical Structure of the Bantu Language Family: Old Challenges, New Insights
UNESCO World Heritage Centre (1986), Great Zimbabwe National Monument
Siyabonga Hadebe (2025), The Colonial Construction of Race in Africa: Debunking Myths and Unravelling Histories of the So-called First Nation Identity

entries.label: Khoisan
entries.summary: A collective label used in scholarship for several communities. Staphorst (2021) notes its historical uses while discussing the naming choices made in the study of nineteenth-century |xam narratives. Hadebe (2025), an opinion column, argues that the label belongs to colonial classification and that a 'First Nation' identity built on it risks reviving colonial divisions. The sources disagree, and neither is a source for how any community names itself.
entries.framing: Treat the label as something outsiders built and ask first how the communities concerned name themselves. Keep both readings visible rather than choosing one silently.

sources.label: Luan Staphorst (2021), Term history: Khoisan / Khoesan
Siyabonga Hadebe (2025), The Colonial Construction of Race in Africa: Debunking Myths and Unravelling Histories of the So-called First Nation Identity

entries.label: Colonial classification of peoples
entries.summary: The practice, described by Hadebe (2025), of sorting African peoples into labels such as Bantu, Nilotes and Khoi, which the column says served to justify control and a racial hierarchy. This is one commentator's argument, and it is recorded as a viewpoint, not as a finding.
entries.framing: Read colonial-era categories as records of what outsiders claimed and why, not as descriptions the people concerned would give of themselves.

sources.label: Siyabonga Hadebe (2025), The Colonial Construction of Race in Africa: Debunking Myths and Unravelling Histories of the So-called First Nation Identity

entries.label: Hamitic theory
entries.summary: Named by Hadebe (2025) among the ideas, together with German scholarship and Hegel's views, that the column blames for denying Africa its own history and crediting outsiders with its achievements. This is one commentator's argument. A peer-reviewed source on the theory itself has not been added yet.
entries.framing: Read it as something outsiders claimed about Africans, and ask who it served. Keep what African scholars say in reply separate from what the theory said, and do not repeat its claims as findings.

sources.label: Siyabonga Hadebe (2025), The Colonial Construction of Race in Africa: Debunking Myths and Unravelling Histories of the So-called First Nation Identity

entries.label: Great Zimbabwe
entries.summary: The UNESCO record gives the meaning of the name as 'the house in stone' and attributes the city to the Shona. Vieri and colleagues (2023) study gold working there and stress local production and agency in its trade.
entries.framing: Begin with the name, the people who gave it and what they made there. Treat outsiders' later accounts of the site as claims to check, not as its history.

sources.label: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (1986), Great Zimbabwe National Monument
Jasmine Vieri et al. (2023), Archaeological science, globalisation, and local agency: gold in Great Zimbabwe

entries.label: Pyramids at Giza
entries.summary: Research focus: describe the Giza pyramids within ancient Egyptian history and use excavated settlement evidence carefully when discussing the people who built them.
entries.framing: Starter framing from the design brief. Specific claims about workforce size and working conditions need source review.

sources.label: Mark Lehner (2001), The 1988/1989 Excavation at Giza

entries.label: Lebombo and Ishango bones
entries.summary: Research focus: distinguish the age and markings of the artefacts from claims about what their markings meant.
entries.framing: Starter framing from the design brief. Locate and review archaeological publications before making a claim about counting or mathematics.

entries.label: African-centred history (Chancellor Williams)
entries.summary: Research focus: present Chancellor Williams's book as an African-centred interpretation of Black Africa's past, attribute each point to him, and read it beside archaeological, linguistic and genetic evidence.
entries.framing: Added because this perspective is central to the project. The book is recorded as critical commentary, not primary evidence. Any specific claim taken from it needs a page reference, a second source, and reviewer sign-off before it can be published.

sources.label: Chancellor Williams (1987), The Destruction of Black Civilization: Great Issues of a Race from 4500 B.C. to 2000 A.D.

categories.othering: Wording that casts people as lesser or as other
categories.outsider: Wording that puts outsiders at the centre of the story

cues.label: primitive, savage, uncivilised
cues.reason: Describes people or societies as lesser or less developed. That is a judgement about them, not a description of what they did.

cues.label: "the natives"
cues.reason: Names people only by contrast with outsiders, not by how they name themselves.

cues.label: tribe, tribal
cues.reason: A catch-all label that can hide distinct nations, kingdoms and languages. Check how the people name themselves.

cues.label: "dark continent"
cues.reason: Presents Africa as unknown or empty until outsiders arrived.

cues.label: "witch doctor"
cues.reason: An outsider's label for healers and spiritual leaders, which hides the roles they actually held.

cues.label: "discovered by" outsiders
cues.reason: Treats a place the people who lived there already knew as new once outsiders reached it.

cues.label: "civilising mission"
cues.reason: Frames outside rule as a gift to the people it ruled.

cues.label: "lost city", "mysterious ruins"
cues.reason: Implies the builders are unknown, which can sideline the people who lived there and their descendants.

cues.label: "must have been built by"
phrases: could not have been built by
cues.reason: Suggests African people could not have done something, so someone else must have.

cues.label: "Hamitic"
cues.reason: Names a theory that credited outside origins for African achievements. See the Hamitic theory note.

cues.label: "opened up Africa"
cues.reason: Describes Africa from the point of view of those who arrived, not those already there.
